summary: Orbit Pulse is a health monitoring system for people who are far from a doctor, such as astronauts on long missions and communities in remote or disaster-hit areas. It tracks heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature and breathing rate, along with environmental risks like cabin CO₂ and radiation dose. Each reading is checked against warning and critical limits, and the system gives a single risk score, a timestamped alert log and plain-language advice. It runs on the device itself, so it still works when communication is slow or missing. This addresses the challenge by catching health problems early when expert help is delayed. It matters because the same tool that protects a crew in space can protect people on Earth who have no nearby clinic.
details:
What does it do? Orbit Pulse is a live dashboard that monitors six readings: heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, breathing rate, cabin CO₂ and radiation dose rate. It shows each one on a card that turns green, amber or red, with a small trend line. A risk score from 0 to 100, an overall crew status and an alert log summarize the situation. Scenario buttons (rest, exercise, high CO₂, solar flare, fever) let users see how the system reacts to different events.

How does it work? Every second, each reading is updated and compared with a warning range and a critical range. A warning adds 14 points to the risk score and a critical reading adds 32, up to 100. The alert log records each change of level with a mission-style timestamp, and pre-written advice appears for the active scenario. In this prototype the values are simulated, so the demo works anywhere. In a real deployment the same logic would take readings from sensors such as a pulse oximeter, a temperature sensor and a CO₂ sensor.

What benefits does it have? It gives early warning, explains what changed in plain language, and keeps working offline. It does not need a specialist to read raw numbers.

What is the intended impact? To keep people safe where medical help is far away, first for space crews and then for remote villages, disaster zones and field workers on Earth.

Tools and technology: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single page, with no external libraries. Fonts: Bricolage Grotesque and Instrument Sans from Google Fonts. Planned hardware: ESP32 or Arduino with MAX30102, MLX90614 and MH-Z19 sensors.

How is it creative? It treats space health and remote health on Earth as one problem, and shows the same system working in both settings. Everything is built to work on the device, so it needs no internet.

Factors we considered: privacy (data stays on the device), low cost, readability for non-experts, and safety. Limits are illustrative and the app is not a medical device.
dataRefs: NASA DONKI – Space Weather Database of Notifications, Knowledge, Information (M1.7 solar flare, 11 Nov 2026)
